claim: Timothy syndrome (TS) is caused by a point mutation in the alternatively spliced exon 8A of the calcium channel Cav1.2.
source: The syndromic autism spectrum disorder (ASD) Timothy syndrome (TS) is caused by a point mutation in the alternatively spliced exon 8A of the calcium channel Cav1.2.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about the genetic cause of Timothy syndrome.

claim: The TS mutation prevents a normal developmental switch in Cav1.2 exon utilization.
source: Using mouse brain and human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), we provide evidence that the TS mutation prevents a normal developmental switch in Cav1.2 exon utilization, resulting in persistent expression of gain-of-function mutant channels during neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experiments in mouse brain and human iPSCs.

claim: The TS mutation results in persistent expression of gain-of-function mutant channels during neuronal differentiation.
source: Using mouse brain and human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), we provide evidence that the TS mutation prevents a normal developmental switch in Cav1.2 exon utilization, resulting in persistent expression of gain-of-function mutant channels during neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experiments in mouse brain and human iPSCs.

claim: The TS mutation reduces the abundance of SATB2-expressing cortical projection neurons in iPSC models.
source: In iPSC models, the TS mutation reduces the abundance of SATB2-expressing cortical projection neurons, leading to excess CTIP2+ neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from iPSC experiments described in the abstract.

claim: The TS mutation leads to excess CTIP2+ neurons in iPSC models.
source: In iPSC models, the TS mutation reduces the abundance of SATB2-expressing cortical projection neurons, leading to excess CTIP2+ neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from iPSC experiments described in the abstract.

claim: Expression of TS-Cav1.2 channels in the embryonic mouse cortex recapitulates differentiation defects in a calcium-dependent manner.
source: We show that expression of TS-Cav1.2 channels in the embryonic mouse cortex recapitulates these differentiation defects in a calcium-dependent manner and that in utero Cav1.2 gain-and-loss of function reciprocally regulates the abundance of these neuronal populations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in utero mouse experiments described in the abstract.

claim: In utero Cav1.2 gain-and-loss of function reciprocally regulates the abundance of SATB2+ and CTIP2+ neuronal populations.
source: We show that expression of TS-Cav1.2 channels in the embryonic mouse cortex recapitulates these differentiation defects in a calcium-dependent manner and that in utero Cav1.2 gain-and-loss of function reciprocally regulates the abundance of these neuronal populations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in utero mouse experiments described in the abstract.

claim: Disruption of developmentally regulated calcium channel splicing patterns instructively alters differentiation in the developing cortex.
source: Our findings support the idea that disruption of developmentally regulated calcium channel splicing patterns instructively alters differentiation in the developing cortex, providing important in vivo insights into the pathophysiology of a syndromic ASD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Genome-wide association studies have identified gain- and loss-of-function mutations in CACNA1C in patients with bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorders.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of patients with bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorders (ASD) have identified gain- and loss-of-function mutations in CACNA1C, the gene encoding the α1C subunit of the voltage-gated L-type calcium channel (LTC) Cav1.2 (Ferreira et al., 2008; Green et al., 2010; Ripke et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous GWAS studies.

claim: CACNA1C encodes the α1C subunit of the voltage-gated L-type calcium channel Cav1.2.
source: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of patients with bipolar disorder, schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorders (ASD) have identified gain- and loss-of-function mutations in CACNA1C, the gene encoding the α1C subunit of the voltage-gated L-type calcium channel (LTC) Cav1.2 (Ferreira et al., 2008; Green et al., 2010; Ripke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the gene product of CACNA1C.

claim: Genetic variants in calcium signaling proteins and voltage-gated calcium channel subunits have been associated with ASD, schizophrenia, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder.
source: Genetic variants in calcium signaling proteins and voltage-gated calcium channel subunits, including the pore-forming α and auxiliary β subunits of Cav1.2, have also been associated with disorders such as ASD, schizophrenia, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (Cross-Disorder Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Timothy syndrome is characterized by cardiac dysfunction, intellectual disability and ASD.
source: Timothy syndrome (TS), a developmental disorder characterized by cardiac dysfunction, intellectual disability and ASD, is caused by a gain-of-function missense mutation in an alternatively spliced exon of Cav1.2 (Splawski et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the clinical features of Timothy syndrome, supported by citation.

claim: The TS mutation G406R is located in exon 8A, which encodes transmembrane segment 6 (IS6) of channel domain 1.
source: The point mutation in classical TS, G406R, is located in exon 8A, which encodes transmembrane segment 6 (IS6) of channel domain 1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the location of the TS mutation.

claim: The G406R mutation causes impaired voltage-dependent channel inactivation.
source: Transcripts containing the G406R mutation encode a channel that exhibits impaired voltage-dependent channel inactivation and, as a result, gives rise to prolonged activity-dependent elevations in intracellular calcium (Splawski et al., 2004; Paşca et al., 2011; Krey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The G406R mutation gives rise to prolonged activity-dependent elevations in intracellular calcium.
source: Transcripts containing the G406R mutation encode a channel that exhibits impaired voltage-dependent channel inactivation and, as a result, gives rise to prolonged activity-dependent elevations in intracellular calcium (Splawski et al., 2004; Paşca et al., 2011; Krey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Immature cells of the embryonic cortex possess a repertoire of ion channels and a chloride resting state that promotes depolarization by GABA.
source: Immature cells of the embryonic cortex possess a repertoire of ion channels and a chloride resting state that promotes depolarization by GABA (Ben-Ari, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Disrupting GABA-induced excitation during the transitional state causes pronounced synaptic and behavioral defects associated with psychiatric disease.
source: Disrupting GABA-induced excitation during this transitional state causes pronounced synaptic and behavioral defects associated with psychiatric disease (Wang and Kriegstein, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: GABA and glutamate depolarization, as well as synchronous calcium fluctuations, play a role in the proliferation of radially clustered neural progenitor cells in the developing mouse cerebral cortex.
source: In situ calcium imaging studies during normal development have suggested a role for GABA and glutamate depolarization, as well as synchronous calcium fluctuations, in the proliferation of radially clustered neural progenitor cells (NPCs) in the developing mouse cerebral cortex (LoTurco et al., 1995; Weissman et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Progressive temporally regulated hyperpolarization of cortical NPCs has been linked to the sequential emergence of distinct laminar fates.
source: More recently, progressive temporally regulated hyperpolarization of cortical NPCs has been linked to the sequential emergence of distinct laminar fates (Vitali et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The TS mutation in Cav1.2 alters the elaboration of dendrites in immature neurons.
source: The TS mutation in Cav1.2 has been shown to alter later events in corticogenesis, including the elaboration of dendrites in immature neurons (Krey et al., 2013) and the radial migration of upper layer neurons (Kamijo et al., 2018), but it remains unclear which channels mediate calcium signals in differentiating cells of the developing cortex and how their activity is controlled during differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The TS mutation in Cav1.2 alters the radial migration of upper layer neurons.
source: The TS mutation in Cav1.2 has been shown to alter later events in corticogenesis, including the elaboration of dendrites in immature neurons (Krey et al., 2013) and the radial migration of upper layer neurons (Kamijo et al., 2018), but it remains unclear which channels mediate calcium signals in differentiating cells of the developing cortex and how their activity is controlled during differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Upon exiting the cell cycle, newborn excitatory neurons sequentially migrate out of the ventricular and subventricular zones to their appropriate laminar destination within the cortex.
source: Upon exiting the cell cycle, newborn excitatory neurons sequentially migrate out of the ventricular and subventricular zones (VZ, SVZ) to their appropriate laminar destination within the cortex (Okano and Temple, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The acquisition of neuronal subtype and laminar identity is regulated in part by subtype-specific genetic programs.
source: The acquisition of neuronal subtype and laminar identity is regulated in part by subtype-specific genetic programs (Molyneaux et al., 2007; Leone et al., 2008; Fame et al., 2011; Srinivasan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The specification of SCPNs requires the expression of the transcription factors FEZF2 and CTIP2.
source: The specification of SCPNs requires the expression of the transcription factors FEZF2 and CTIP2, whereas persistent expression of the DNA-binding protein SATB2 is a hallmark of callosal projection neuron (CPN) identity (Arlotta et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2005; Molyneaux et al., 2005; Alcamo et al., 2008; Arlotta et al., 2008; Britanova et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Persistent expression of SATB2 is a hallmark of callosal projection neuron (CPN) identity.
source: The specification of SCPNs requires the expression of the transcription factors FEZF2 and CTIP2, whereas persistent expression of the DNA-binding protein SATB2 is a hallmark of callosal projection neuron (CPN) identity (Arlotta et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2005; Molyneaux et al., 2005; Alcamo et al., 2008; Arlotta et al., 2008; Britanova et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TS patient-derived cells displayed prolonged intracellular calcium elevations in response to depolarization.
source: Using a human iPSC platform, our laboratory previously generated neurons from patients with TS. Patient cells displayed prolonged intracellular calcium elevations in response to depolarization and deficits in calcium signaling.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors' laboratory.

claim: TS patient-derived cells displayed deficits in calcium signaling.
source: Using a human iPSC platform, our laboratory previously generated neurons from patients with TS. Patient cells displayed prolonged intracellular calcium elevations in response to depolarization and deficits in calcium signaling.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors' laboratory.

claim: Changes in gene expression in TS patient cells suggested a decrease in CPNs and proportional increase in SCPNs.
source: The resulting changes in gene expression suggested a decrease in CPNs and proportional increase in SCPNs (Paşca et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The differentiation of NPCs into post-mitotic neurons is accompanied by a shift in Cav1.2 exon utilization from exon 8A to exon 8.
source: Here, using both mouse brain and human iPSC-derived cortical cultures, we show that the differentiation of NPCs into post-mitotic neurons is accompanied by a shift in Cav1.2 exon utilization from exon 8A to exon 8.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experiments in mouse brain and human iPSCs.

claim: iPSC-derived cells from individuals with TS fail to undergo the developmental shift to exon 8 utilization.
source: iPSC-derived cells from individuals with TS fail to undergo this developmental shift to exon 8 utilization and continue to express gain-of-function channels containing the mutant exon 8A during neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experiments with TS patient-derived iPSCs.

claim: TS patient-derived cells continue to express gain-of-function channels containing the mutant exon 8A during neuronal differentiation.
source: iPSC-derived cells from individuals with TS fail to undergo this developmental shift to exon 8 utilization and continue to express gain-of-function channels containing the mutant exon 8A during neuronal differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experiments with TS patient-derived iPSCs.

claim: Persistent expression of TS gain-of-function channels is sufficient to phenocopy the differentiation defects observed in patient-derived neurons.
source: In a series of in vivo experiments in mice, we go on to show that persistent expression of TS gain-of-function channels is alone sufficient to phenocopy the differentiation defects observed in patient-derived neurons, altering the expression of fate determinants during neuronal differentiation in a calcium-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vivo mouse experiments.

claim: TS channels alter the expression of fate determinants during neuronal differentiation in a calcium-dependent manner.
source: In a series of in vivo experiments in mice, we go on to show that persistent expression of TS gain-of-function channels is alone sufficient to phenocopy the differentiation defects observed in patient-derived neurons, altering the expression of fate determinants during neuronal differentiation in a calcium-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in vivo mouse experiments.

claim: During corticogenesis, mRNA expression of exon 8A declined after birth.
source: During corticogenesis, mRNA expression of exon 8A declined after birth, whereas exon 8-containing transcripts increased to levels that plateaued in adulthood (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Exon 8-containing transcripts increased to levels that plateaued in adulthood during corticogenesis.
source: During corticogenesis, mRNA expression of exon 8A declined after birth, whereas exon 8-containing transcripts increased to levels that plateaued in adulthood (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: In postnatal cortex, the ratio of exon 8A/exon 8 declined markedly.
source: In postnatal cortex, the ratio of exon 8A/exon 8 declined markedly to levels consistent with the significantly higher expression of exon 8 in post-mitotic neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The abundance of exon 8A-containing transcripts decreases per cell to nearly undetectable levels between embryonic day 18 (E18) and postnatal day 14 (P14).
source: qRT-PCR on individual cortical cells using Fluidigm dynamic arrays further confirmed that the abundance of exon 8A-containing transcripts decreases per cell to nearly undetectable levels between embryonic day 18 (E18) and postnatal day 14 (P14) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: This is based on single-cell qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f.

claim: At E14, expression of exon 8A transcripts was highest in the VZ/SVZ of the developing cortex and in ventral structures such as the ganglionic eminences and the striatum.
source: At E14, expression of exon 8A transcripts was highest in the VZ/SVZ of the developing cortex and in ventral structures such as the ganglionic eminences and the striatum (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Exon 8 mRNA was more broadly expressed in the developing brain.
source: Exon 8 mRNA was more broadly expressed in the developing brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1g.

claim: At E18, exon 8A expression persisted in the VZs of the dorsal and ventral forebrain.
source: At E18, exon 8A expression persisted in the VZs of the dorsal and ventral forebrain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1h.

claim: A dramatic increase in exon 8 expression occurs upon neuronal differentiation of control iPSC-derived NPCs.
source: Using previously established protocols (Paşca et al., 2011), we differentiated iPSCs from control subjects into dorsal forebrain NPCs and excitatory neurons and observed a dramatic increase in exon 8 expression upon neuronal differentiation, comparable to what we saw in mouse (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data from human iPSC-derived cells shown in Figure 1c.

claim: In human fetal cortex, exon 8 expression increased to levels greater than exon 8A as development progressed.
source: Similarly, in human fetal cortex, exon 8 expression increased to levels greater than exon 8A as development progressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data from human fetal cortex shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Exon 8A-containing Cav1.2 transcripts are enriched in undifferentiated progenitors and young neurons.
source: Together, our data in mouse and human support the idea that exon 8A-containing Cav1.2 transcripts are enriched in undifferentiated progenitors and young neurons, indicating that the TS mutation may act in immature cells to influence cell fate decisions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression data in mouse and human.

claim: The TS mutation may act in immature cells to influence cell fate decisions.
source: Together, our data in mouse and human support the idea that exon 8A-containing Cav1.2 transcripts are enriched in undifferentiated progenitors and young neurons, indicating that the TS mutation may act in immature cells to influence cell fate decisions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the expression pattern of exon 8A.

claim: The G > A nucleotide substitution that causes the TS mutation occurs in the penultimate nucleotide of exon 8A.
source: The G > A nucleotide substitution that causes the TS mutation occurs in the penultimate nucleotide of exon 8A, placing it squarely in position to influence splicing of this exon and its counterpart exon 8.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the location of the TS mutation.

claim: The TS mutation is positioned to influence splicing of exon 8A and exon 8.
source: The G > A nucleotide substitution that causes the TS mutation occurs in the penultimate nucleotide of exon 8A, placing it squarely in position to influence splicing of this exon and its counterpart exon 8.
evidence: This is an inference based on the location of the mutation in the splice acceptor site.

claim: TS patient-derived NPCs and neurons exhibit a pronounced splicing defect that favors inclusion of the mutant exon 8A in CACNA1C transcripts.
source: To investigate this possibility, we performed qRT-PCR on TS patient-derived NPCs and neurons. We observed a pronounced splicing defect in patient cells that favored inclusion of the mutant exon 8A in CACNA1C transcripts (Figure 1d–h).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data from TS patient-derived cells shown in Figure 1d–h.

claim: The upregulation of exon 8 that typically occurs with neuronal differentiation was abrogated in TS neurons.
source: The upregulation of exon 8 that typically occurs with neuronal differentiation was abrogated in TS neurons (Figure 1d), and the expression of exon 8A as compared to exon 8 was markedly increased across patient-derived NPC lines (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data from TS patient-derived cells shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The expression of exon 8A as compared to exon 8 was markedly increased across patient-derived NPC lines.
source: The upregulation of exon 8 that typically occurs with neuronal differentiation was abrogated in TS neurons (Figure 1d), and the expression of exon 8A as compared to exon 8 was markedly increased across patient-derived NPC lines (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data from TS patient-derived cells shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The exon 8A/exon 8 ratio in patient cells was significantly increased at the population level.
source: Moreover, the exon 8A/exon 8 ratio in patient cells was significantly increased at the population level (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data from TS patient-derived cells shown in Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 1j.

claim: The proportion of individual neurons expressing exon 8A in TS patients was dramatically increased compared to controls.
source: Single-cell qRT-PCR using Fluidigm arrays revealed that the proportion of individual neurons expressing exon 8A in TS patients was dramatically increased compared to controls (Figure 1g), suggesting continued expression of the TS mutation in a significant fraction of differentiating cells.
evidence: This is based on single-cell qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The proportion of total neurons in patients and controls was unaltered, as measured by the proportion of cells expressing NCAM.
source: Notably, the proportion of total neurons in patients and controls was unaltered, as measured by the proportion of cells expressing neural cell adhesion molecule (NCAM) (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is based on single-cell qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: The TS mutation in exon 8A favors the inclusion of exon 8A in CACNA1C transcripts at the expense of exon 8 expression.
source: These data suggest that the TS mutation in exon 8A favors the inclusion of exon 8A in CACNA1C transcripts at the expense of exon 8 expression (Figure 1i).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the splicing data in TS patient cells.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining for Cav1.2 in embryonic mouse cortex demonstrated weak expression of Cav1.2 channels in NPCs lining the ventricles with significantly higher levels in neurons in the cortical plate, as early as E11.
source: Consistent with our RNA expression analyses, immunofluorescence staining for Cav1.2 in embryonic mouse cortex demonstrated weak expression of Cav1.2 channels in NPCs lining the ventricles with significantly higher levels in neurons in the cortical plate (CP), as early as E11 (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Within the VZ, Cav1.2 expression was not uniform across cells.
source: Within the VZ, Cav1.2 expression was not uniform across cells (Figure 2b), as expression of the channel was restricted to a subset of NPCs early in corticogenesis and subsequently spread to a majority of cells by E16.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Expression of Cav1.2 was restricted to a subset of NPCs early in corticogenesis and subsequently spread to a majority of cells by E16.
source: Within the VZ, Cav1.2 expression was not uniform across cells (Figure 2b), as expression of the channel was restricted to a subset of NPCs early in corticogenesis and subsequently spread to a majority of cells by E16.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Late in corticogenesis, Cav1.2 levels increased dramatically.
source: Late in corticogenesis, Cav1.2 levels increased dramatically (Figure 2c), likely owing to elevated expression of the channel in post-mitotic neuroblasts and neurons.
evidence: This is based on Western blot data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: GABA-induced calcium rises in NPCs and immature neurons were nearly completely abrogated by the application of 5 μM nimodipine, a selective LTC blocker.
source: We observed calcium rises in NPCs and immature neurons induced by depolarization with 30 μM GABA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–d) in a fraction of cells (20–55% in our experiments), in line with previous studies using GABA to depolarize NPCs in slices of embryonic cortex (LoTurco et al., 1995). GABA-induced calcium rises were nearly completely abrogated by the application of 5 μM nimodipine, a selective LTC blocker (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,d), indicating that LTCs control calcium signals in NPCs and young neurons in the developing cortex.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–d.

claim: LTCs control calcium signals in NPCs and young neurons in the developing cortex.
source: GABA-induced calcium rises were nearly completely abrogated by the application of 5 μM nimodipine, a selective LTC blocker (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,d), indicating that LTCs control calcium signals in NPCs and young neurons in the developing cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the nimodipine blockade experiment.

claim: Cav1.2 protein was robustly expressed throughout the cerebral wall in gestational week (GW) 16 human cortex, with lower expression in the VZ and inner SVZ.
source: Extending these analyses to human, we found that Cav1.2 protein was robustly expressed throughout the cerebral wall in gestational week (GW) 16 human cortex, with lower expression in the VZ and inner SVZ (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e), similar to our results in mouse.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data from human fetal cortex shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Cav1.2 was strongly expressed in the outer SVZ (oSVZ) in GW16 human cortex.
source: Of note, Cav1.2 was strongly expressed in the outer SVZ (oSVZ, Figure 2—figure supplement 1e), an expanded neurogenic zone in the primate lineage containing newly identified classes of progenitor cells (Fietz et al., 2010; Hansen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence data from human fetal cortex shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Cav1.2 is expressed at the right time and place to influence the process of neuronal differentiation and subtype specification.
source: Together, our observations in mouse and human cortex indicate that Cav1.2 is expressed at the right time and place to influence the process of neuronal differentiation and subtype specification.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression pattern of Cav1.2 in mouse and human cortex.

claim: Calcium elevations resulting from expression of TS channels in Neuro2A cells were more sustained as compared to expression of channels without the mutation.
source: Consistent with previous work demonstrating that the TS mutation prolongs voltage-dependent channel inactivation and depolarization-induced calcium rises (Splawski et al., 2004; Paşca et al., 2011), calcium elevations resulting from expression of TS channels in Neuro2A cells were more sustained as compared to expression of channels without the mutation (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data from transfected Neuro2A cells shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Cav1.2-TS electroporation dramatically reduced the abundance of SATB2-expressing EGFP+ cells and increased CTIP2 expression.
source: Cav1.2-TS electroporation dramatically reduced the abundance of SATB2-expressing EGFP+ cells and increased CTIP2 expression, consistent with our previous gene expression findings in human TS-derived neurons (Paşca et al., 2011) (Figure 2f–g and i, Figure 2—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: This is based on in utero electroporation data shown in Figure 2f–g and i, Figure 2—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Electroporation of calcium-impermeable Cav1.2-TS-4EQ mutant channels did not alter the relative abundance of CTIP2- and SATB2-expressing populations.
source: Importantly, electroporation of calcium-impermeable Cav1.2-TS-4EQ mutant channels did not alter the relative abundance of CTIP2- and SATB2-expressing populations (Figure 2d,h–i, Figure 2—figure supplement 1i), indicating that calcium influx through Cav1.2 is required for the differentiation defects observed with expression of the TS mutation.
evidence: This is based on in utero electroporation data shown in Figure 2d,h–i, Figure 2—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Calcium influx through Cav1.2 is required for the differentiation defects observed with expression of the TS mutation.
source: Importantly, electroporation of calcium-impermeable Cav1.2-TS-4EQ mutant channels did not alter the relative abundance of CTIP2- and SATB2-expressing populations (Figure 2d,h–i, Figure 2—figure supplement 1i), indicating that calcium influx through Cav1.2 is required for the differentiation defects observed with expression of the TS mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pore mutant experiment.

claim: Electroporation of control IRES-GFP, Cav1.2-TS, and Cav1.2-TS-4EQ constructs did not alter the relative abundance of PAX6+ radial glia and TRB2+ intermediate progenitors in the VZ/SVZ at E15.5.
source: To rule out the possibility that these differentiation defects resulted from earlier Cav1.2-dependent alterations of the NPC pool, we electroporated control IRES-GFP, Cav1.2-TS, and Cav1.2-TS-4EQ constructs into wild-type pregnant mice at E13.5 and quantified the proportion of PAX6+ radial glia and TRB2+ intermediate progenitors in the VZ/SVZ at E15.5 (Figure 2j, Figure 2—figure supplement 1j). We observed no alterations in the relative abundance of progenitor types with these manipulations, suggesting that calcium through Cav1.2 impacts the onset of determinants of cortical neuron projection identity in differentiating NPCs (Figure 2k–n, Figure 2—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: This is based on in utero electroporation data shown in Figure 2k–n, Figure 2—figure supplement 1j.

claim: Calcium through Cav1.2 impacts the onset of determinants of cortical neuron projection identity in differentiating NPCs.
source: We observed no alterations in the relative abundance of progenitor types with these manipulations, suggesting that calcium through Cav1.2 impacts the onset of determinants of cortical neuron projection identity in differentiating NPCs (Figure 2k–n, Figure 2—figure supplement 1j).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of effect on progenitor populations.

claim: Modulating calcium levels in differentiating cells plays a role in the choice between adoption of CTIP2 or SATB2 expression in the developing cortex.
source: Collectively, our observations thus far suggest that modulating calcium levels in differentiating cells plays a role in the choice between adoption of CTIP2 or SATB2 expression in the developing cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gain-of-function experiments.

claim: In utero gain of function of Cav1.2-WT and Cav1.2-WT-4EQ channels at E13.5 resulted in a calcium-dependent reduction in SATB2-expressing CPNs in the cortical plate at E17.5 and a commensurate increase in CTIP2+ SCPNs.
source: In line with this idea, in utero gain of function of Cav1.2-WT and Cav1.2-WT-4EQ channels at E13.5 also resulted in a calcium-dependent reduction in SATB2-expressing CPNs in the cortical plate at E17.5 and a commensurate increase in CTIP2+ SCPNs (Figure 3a–d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on in utero electroporation data shown in Figure 3a–d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Expression of Cav1.2-WT channels did not change the relative proportion of radial glia and intermediate progenitor populations in the VZ/SVZ.
source: As with expression of Cav1.2-TS channels, we also assessed NPC distribution in the VZ/SVZ among electroporated cells and found no changes in the relative proportion of radial glia and intermediate progenitor populations that give rise to immature neurons (Figure 3e–h, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is based on in utero electroporation data shown in Figure 3e–h, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Loss of only one copy of Cav1.2 (Cacna1c+/-) resulted in a significant reduction in the proportion of CTIP2-expressing EGFP+ cells and an increase in SATB2-expressing cells in the CP.
source: Loss of only one copy of Cav1.2 (Cacna1c+/-) resulted in a significant reduction in the proportion of CTIP2-expressing EGFP+ cells and an increase in SATB2-expressing cells in the CP (Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a), opposite to what we found with TS channels and Cav1.2 gain of function.
evidence: This is based on in utero loss-of-function data shown in Figure 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Cav1.2 loss resulted in decreased expression of TBR1.
source: In addition to the observed effects on CTIP2 and SATB2, Cav1.2 loss also resulted in decreased expression of TBR1 (Figure 4e–f), a transcription factor required for differentiation of layer VI cortico-thalamic projection neurons that is also expressed at lower levels downstream of SATB2 in upper layer neurons (Srinivasan et al., 2012; Hevner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on in utero loss-of-function data shown in Figure 4e–f.

claim: TBR1 is a transcription factor required for differentiation of layer VI cortico-thalamic projection neurons.
source: In addition to the observed effects on CTIP2 and SATB2, Cav1.2 loss also resulted in decreased expression of TBR1 (Figure 4e–f), a transcription factor required for differentiation of layer VI cortico-thalamic projection neurons that is also expressed at lower levels downstream of SATB2 in upper layer neurons (Srinivasan et al., 2012; Hevner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TBR1 is expressed at lower levels downstream of SATB2 in upper layer neurons.
source: In addition to the observed effects on CTIP2 and SATB2, Cav1.2 loss also resulted in decreased expression of TBR1 (Figure 4e–f), a transcription factor required for differentiation of layer VI cortico-thalamic projection neurons that is also expressed at lower levels downstream of SATB2 in upper layer neurons (Srinivasan et al., 2012; Hevner et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Bicuculine- or glutamate-induced increases in excitation upregulate TBR1 expression in adult brain.
source: This result is consistent with previous studies in adult brain suggesting that bicuculine- or glutamate-induced increases in excitation upregulate TBR1 expression (Chuang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Recent work has described significant CACNA1C transcript diversity in the adult human brain.
source: Recent work has described significant CACNA1C transcript diversity in the adult human brain (Clark et al., 2020), and previous studies have suggested temporal regulation of the splicing of some exons of Cav1.2 in both the heart and brain (Diebold et al., 1992; Tang et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Previous studies have suggested temporal regulation of the splicing of some exons of Cav1.2 in both the heart and brain.
source: Recent work has described significant CACNA1C transcript diversity in the adult human brain (Clark et al., 2020), and previous studies have suggested temporal regulation of the splicing of some exons of Cav1.2 in both the heart and brain (Diebold et al., 1992; Tang et al., 2009; Tang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The inclusion of exons 9* and 33 in Cav1.2 transcripts is inversely regulated during embryonic brain development.
source: For example, the inclusion of exons 9* and 33 in Cav1.2 transcripts, which confer distinct physiological channel properties, is inversely regulated during embryonic brain development (Tang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Transcript scanning has revealed tissue-specific splicing preferences in smooth muscle and heart.
source: In smooth muscle and heart, transcript scanning has also revealed tissue-specific splicing preferences, suggesting that precise utilization of exons is influenced by combinatorial and coordinated splicing mechanisms (Tang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Exons 8 and 8A in the CACNA1C gene are dynamically regulated during mouse and human cortical development.
source: Here, we found that exons 8 and 8A in the CACNA1C gene are dynamically regulated during mouse and human cortical development, consistent with a previous study in the mouse identifying an exon 8 splice repressor (Tang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on expression data.

claim: Exons 8 and 8A are expressed in a mutually exclusive fashion.
source: These exons are expressed in a mutually exclusive fashion, and we show in this study that exon 8A is expressed at lower levels predominantly in undifferentiated cells early in development, whereas expression of exon 8 increases as neurons mature.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on expression data.

claim: Exon 8A is expressed at lower levels predominantly in undifferentiated cells early in development.
source: These exons are expressed in a mutually exclusive fashion, and we show in this study that exon 8A is expressed at lower levels predominantly in undifferentiated cells early in development, whereas expression of exon 8 increases as neurons mature.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on expression data.

claim: Expression of exon 8 increases as neurons mature.
source: These exons are expressed in a mutually exclusive fashion, and we show in this study that exon 8A is expressed at lower levels predominantly in undifferentiated cells early in development, whereas expression of exon 8 increases as neurons mature.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on expression data.

claim: Previous studies investigating human Cav1.2 variants differing only in the inclusion of exon 8 or 8A report that exchanging these two exons yields channel isoforms with similar electrophysiological properties.
source: Previous studies investigating human Cav1.2 variants differing only in the inclusion of exon 8 or 8A report that exchanging these two exons yields channel isoforms with similar electrophysiological properties and only subtle changes in sensitivity to dihydropyridine calcium channel inhibitors (Welling et al., 1997; Zühlke et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TS mutation causes a pronounced loss of voltage-dependent inactivation when introduced into either exon 8 or 8A.
source: By contrast, the TS mutation causes a pronounced loss of voltage-dependent inactivation (VDI) when introduced into either exon 8 or 8A. This results in persistent calcium influx through Cav1.2 channels upon depolarization and accompanying deficits in calcium signaling and activity-dependent gene expression (Splawski et al., 2004; Paşca et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TS mutation results in persistent calcium influx through Cav1.2 channels upon depolarization.
source: By contrast, the TS mutation causes a pronounced loss of voltage-dependent inactivation (VDI) when introduced into either exon 8 or 8A. This results in persistent calcium influx through Cav1.2 channels upon depolarization and accompanying deficits in calcium signaling and activity-dependent gene expression (Splawski et al., 2004; Paşca et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TS mutation causes accompanying deficits in calcium signaling and activity-dependent gene expression.
source: By contrast, the TS mutation causes a pronounced loss of voltage-dependent inactivation (VDI) when introduced into either exon 8 or 8A. This results in persistent calcium influx through Cav1.2 channels upon depolarization and accompanying deficits in calcium signaling and activity-dependent gene expression (Splawski et al., 2004; Paşca et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TS mutation changes Cav1.2 splicing by inducing a shift that favors extended use of exon 8A in patient cells.
source: Here, we show that the TS mutation changes Cav1.2 splicing by inducing a shift that favors extended use of exon 8A in patient cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on splicing data from patient cells.

claim: The TS mutation not only increases calcium influx by impairing VDI, but also ensures that gain-of-function channels containing the TS mutation continue to be expressed during differentiation by promoting continued expression of exon 8A.
source: The TS mutation thus not only increases calcium influx by impairing VDI, but also, by promoting continued expression of exon 8A, it ensures that gain-of-function channels containing the TS mutation continue to be expressed during differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the splicing and functional data.

claim: The change in splicing caused by the TS mutation likely results from the fact that the TS mutation lies in the splice acceptor site of exon 8A, making it favored relative to the splice acceptor site of exon 8.
source: This change in splicing likely results from the fact that the TS mutation lies in the splice acceptor site of exon 8A, making it favored relative to the splice acceptor site of exon 8.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on the location of the mutation.

claim: Continued inclusion of exon 8A prevents the change in CACNA1C splicing that would lead to expression of the wild-type channel at the appropriate time in development.
source: Continued inclusion of exon 8A also prevents the change in CACNA1C splicing that would lead to expression of the wild-type channel at the appropriate time in development.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the splicing defect observed in patient cells.

claim: Failure of the developmental splicing switch in TS alters the relative abundance of channels containing WT and mutant exons during development to contribute to cellular phenotypes caused by the mutation.
source: Failure of this developmental splicing switch in TS alters the relative abundance of channels containing WT and mutant exons during development to contribute to cellular phenotypes caused by the mutation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the splicing and phenotypic data.

claim: The developmental difference in exon utilization could explain the phenotypic differences observed between patients with the TS mutation in exon 8A and those in exon 8.
source: While the full mechanistic impact of this alteration in splicing needs further investigation, the developmental difference in exon utilization reported here could explain the phenotypic differences observed between patients with the TS mutation in exon 8A and those in exon 8.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the splicing findings.

claim: Persistent expression of the TS mutation, owing to extended inclusion of exon 8A, would likely result in elevated activity-dependent calcium signaling as immature cells transition from NPC to post-mitotic neuron.
source: As the TS mutation is known to prolong channel inactivation and thus intracellular calcium rises in response to depolarization, we reasoned that persistent expression of the TS mutation, owing to extended inclusion of exon 8A, would likely result in elevated activity-dependent calcium signaling as immature cells transition from NPC to post-mitotic neuron.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known effects of the TS mutation and the splicing defect.

claim: Altered calcium dynamics resulting from persistent TS mutation expression could give rise to the differentiation defects observed in TS.
source: We further hypothesized that these altered calcium dynamics could give rise to the differentiation defects observed in TS.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested in the study.

claim: Neurons with distinct gene expression profiles, physiological properties, and projection patterns can be generated concomitantly during development and ultimately inhabit the same cortical layer.
source: It is becoming increasingly evident that neurons with distinct gene expression profiles, physiological properties, and projection patterns can be generated concomitantly during development and ultimately inhabit the same cortical layer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cortical development.

claim: In layer V, interhemispheric neurons that send projections through the corpus callosum to the contralateral hemisphere (callosal projection neurons, CPNs) are born concurrently with corticofugal neurons that send axons to subcortical structures and the spinal cord (subcerebral projection neurons, SCPNs).
source: This observation is best exemplified in layer V, where a complex network of mutually repressive transcription factors sets the stage for the generation of SATB2-expressing CPNs and CTIP2-expressing SCPNs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about layer V neuron development.

claim: Introducing TS-Cav1.2 calcium channels into mouse NPCs in utero reduces the fraction of SATB2-expressing cells.
source: Here we show that introducing TS-Cav1.2 calcium channels into mouse NPCs in utero reduces the fraction of SATB2-expressing cells, altering the ratio of early-born cortico-cortico CPNs relative to subcortically projecting SCPN neurons in the developing cortex without changing the abundance of progenitor subtypes that give rise to these cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in utero experiments.

claim: Introducing TS-Cav1.2 calcium channels into mouse NPCs in utero alters the ratio of early-born cortico-cortico CPNs relative to subcortically projecting SCPN neurons in the developing cortex.
source: Here we show that introducing TS-Cav1.2 calcium channels into mouse NPCs in utero reduces the fraction of SATB2-expressing cells, altering the ratio of early-born cortico-cortico CPNs relative to subcortically projecting SCPN neurons in the developing cortex without changing the abundance of progenitor subtypes that give rise to these cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in utero experiments.

claim: Introducing TS-Cav1.2 calcium channels into mouse NPCs in utero does not change the abundance of progenitor subtypes that give rise to CPNs and SCPNs.
source: Here we show that introducing TS-Cav1.2 calcium channels into mouse NPCs in utero reduces the fraction of SATB2-expressing cells, altering the ratio of early-born cortico-cortico CPNs relative to subcortically projecting SCPN neurons in the developing cortex without changing the abundance of progenitor subtypes that give rise to these cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from in utero experiments.

claim: The TS-Cav1.2 channels introduced in utero result in sustained calcium elevations as compared to channels that do not express the TS mutation.
source: Our calcium imaging data, consistent with previous studies, confirms that the TS-Cav1.2 channels we introduced in utero result in sustained calcium elevations as compared to channels that do not express the TS mutation.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data from the study.

claim: Channels that do not carry calcium do not affect the fraction of SATB2-expressing neurons.
source: Collectively, the suppression of SATB2 identity resulting from expression of these TS-Cav1.2 channels, together with the finding that channels that do not carry calcium do not affect the fraction of SATB2-expressing neurons, support the idea that intracellular calcium levels influence the expression of neuronal fate determinants in the developing cortex.
evidence: This is based on the pore mutant experiments.

claim: Intracellular calcium levels influence the expression of neuronal fate determinants in the developing cortex.
source: Collectively, the suppression of SATB2 identity resulting from expression of these TS-Cav1.2 channels, together with the finding that channels that do not carry calcium do not affect the fraction of SATB2-expressing neurons, support the idea that intracellular calcium levels influence the expression of neuronal fate determinants in the developing cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gain-of-function and pore mutant experiments.

claim: Persistent elevations in calcium resulting from aberrant channel splicing and continued expression of mutant channels may underlie the defects in cortical differentiation seen in TS.
source: Moreover, these data suggest that persistent elevations in calcium resulting from aberrant channel splicing and continued expression of mutant channels may underlie the defects in cortical differentiation seen in TS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined splicing and functional data.

claim: Calcium may play an important role in the differentiation of cortical neurons.
source: The idea that calcium may play an important role in the differentiation of cortical neurons is further supported by the Cav1.2 gain- and loss-of-function studies in our study and is consistent with our previous work demonstrating that human iPSC-derived TS cortical neurons have reduced expression of SATB2 and increased expression of CTIP2 (Paşca et al., 2011; Krey et al., 2013), in addition to deregulated calcium signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gain- and loss-of-function experiments and previous work.

claim: Human iPSC-derived TS cortical neurons have reduced expression of SATB2 and increased expression of CTIP2.
source: The idea that calcium may play an important role in the differentiation of cortical neurons is further supported by the Cav1.2 gain- and loss-of-function studies in our study and is consistent with our previous work demonstrating that human iPSC-derived TS cortical neurons have reduced expression of SATB2 and increased expression of CTIP2 (Paşca et al., 2011; Krey et al., 2013), in addition to deregulated calcium signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cav1.2 protein is expressed at relatively low levels in the ventricular zone and in only a fraction of NPCs.
source: It should be noted here, however, that our expression and calcium imaging data suggest that Cav1.2 protein is expressed at relatively low levels in the ventricular zone and in only a fraction of NPCs.
evidence: This is based on the expression and imaging data from the study.

claim: Cav1.2 gain of function primarily occurs as NPCs exit the cell cycle and initiate differentiation.
source: We suspect, based on how long it would likely take to express functional channels at the cell membrane in our in utero electroporation experiments, that Cav1.2 gain of function primarily occurs as NPCs exit the cell cycle and initiate differentiation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the timing of channel expression.

claim: Elevated calcium is likely behind the changes in the relative abundance of CTIP2- and SATB2-expressing populations.
source: Despite this possibility, our findings collectively reinforce the idea that elevated calcium is likely behind the changes we see in the relative abundance of CTIP2- and SATB2-expressing populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental findings.

claim: FEZF2 expression can be induced by brief neuronal activation.
source: FEZF2 expression, for example, can be induced by brief neuronal activation (Tyssowski et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In differentiating keratinocytes, CTIP2 degradation appears to be dependent on intracellular calcium levels.
source: In differentiating keratinocytes, CTIP2 degradation appears to be dependent on intracellular calcium levels (Zhang et al., 2012a), whereas in T cell fate commitment, MAPK signaling and sumoylation regulate CTIP2 activity in a coordinated fashion (Zhang et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In T cell fate commitment, MAPK signaling and sumoylation regulate CTIP2 activity in a coordinated fashion.
source: In differentiating keratinocytes, CTIP2 degradation appears to be dependent on intracellular calcium levels (Zhang et al., 2012a), whereas in T cell fate commitment, MAPK signaling and sumoylation regulate CTIP2 activity in a coordinated fashion (Zhang et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: CTIP2 associates with neuronal BAF (mSWI/SNF) chromatin remodeling complexes.
source: Alternatively, calcium signaling may regulate the activity of subunits of neuronal chromatin remodeling complexes, including neuronal BAF (mSWI/SNF) complexes (Aizawa, 2004), with which CTIP2 itself associates.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The changes in cortical excitatory neuron differentiation observed upon expression of TS channels significantly contribute to the neurodevelopmental phenotypes associated with TS.
source: We propose that the changes in cortical excitatory neuron differentiation that we observe upon expression of TS channels significantly contribute to the neurodevelopmental phenotypes associated with TS.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Altered channel splicing and persistent expression of the G406R mutation may cause ASD and intellectual disability in TS patients by altering the ratio of cortico-cortico and subcerebral projection neurons in the cortex.
source: It is tempting to speculate that one way in which altered channel splicing and persistent expression of the G406R mutation cause ASD and intellectual disability in TS patients is by altering the ratio of cortico-cortico and subcerebral projection neurons in the cortex.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The TS mutation affects later developmental processes in the cortex like dendritic arborization and neuronal migration.
source: This is unlikely to be the only mechanism by which the TS mutation contributes to ASD phenotypes, as other studies have demonstrated significant effects of the mutation on later developmental processes in the cortex like dendritic arborization and neuronal migration (Krey et al., 2013; Kamijo et al., 2018), which are also likely to affect circuits that control learning and social behavior in patients.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells outside the developing cortex, such as striatal projection neurons, express exon 8A during embryonic development.
source: Our in situ hybridization experiments suggest that cells outside the developing cortex, such as striatal projection neurons, express exon 8A during embryonic development, as do immature cells in the germinal zones that give rise to cortical interneuron populations and nuclei of the basal ganglia.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data from the study.

claim: Immature cells in the germinal zones that give rise to cortical interneuron populations and nuclei of the basal ganglia express exon 8A during embryonic development.
source: Our in situ hybridization experiments suggest that cells outside the developing cortex, such as striatal projection neurons, express exon 8A during embryonic development, as do immature cells in the germinal zones that give rise to cortical interneuron populations and nuclei of the basal ganglia.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data from the study.

claim: The early development of other cell types is likely to be influenced by the TS mutation.
source: This observation indicates that the early development of other cell types is also likely to be influenced by the TS mutation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern of exon 8A in other cell types.

claim: Cortical interneurons derived from TS patient cells display abnormal migration.
source: Indeed, using an iPSC spheroid platform, we have shown that cortical interneurons derived from TS patient cells display abnormal migration (Birey et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Calcium influences the differentiation of excitatory neurons in the cortex.
source: Our study provides evidence that calcium influences the differentiation of excitatory neurons in the cortex and that the expression of Cav1.2 channels containing the TS mutation in differentiating cells may underlie changes in neuronal circuitry that contribute to intellectual disability and ASD in TS patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental findings.

claim: The expression of Cav1.2 channels containing the TS mutation in differentiating cells may underlie changes in neuronal circuitry that contribute to intellectual disability and ASD in TS patients.
source: Our study provides evidence that calcium influences the differentiation of excitatory neurons in the cortex and that the expression of Cav1.2 channels containing the TS mutation in differentiating cells may underlie changes in neuronal circuitry that contribute to intellectual disability and ASD in TS patients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental findings.
